checks.question: Has the lender screened the party, its directors and its senior managers against every sanctions list the lender must follow, and kept the result with its date and the lists used?
checks.assumption: The party and the people who direct it have been screened against every list the lender must follow
checks.if_unknown: A party that has not been screened is not known to be clear.
checks.note: The lists usually include those of the United Nations, the European Union, the United States and the United Kingdom, and those of the lender's own country. Owners and controllers are parties of their own and get this check themselves. If the search finds nothing, record what was searched, where and when.

checks.question: Is the party, or any of its directors or senior managers, named on a sanctions list, or owned or controlled by someone who is?
checks.assumption: Neither the party nor anyone who directs, owns or controls it is under sanctions
checks.if_unknown: A possible match that has not been cleared is not a no.
checks.note: A match on a name alone is checked against the date of birth, the nationality and the address before it is recorded as a yes or as a no. If the search finds nothing, record what was searched, where and when.

checks.question: In the last three years, has the party sold to, bought from, shipped through, banked in or been paid from a country or territory under an embargo on trade or payments, or dealt with a person or a company on a sanctions list?
checks.assumption: The party's business does not touch a country under embargo or a person under sanctions
checks.ask: In the last three years, have you sold to, bought from or been paid from a country under embargo, or dealt with anyone on a sanctions list? Please include sales through agents and distributors.
checks.note: Dealings that a licence or an exemption allows still count: answer yes and say which. Look at where the goods end up, not only at where the first buyer sits.

checks.question: Were all those dealings allowed under the sanctions that bind the party and the lender (a licence, an exemption, a wind-down period), as confirmed in writing by a lawyer or by the authority?
checks.assumption: Every dealing with a country under embargo or a person under sanctions was allowed, and a lawyer or the authority has confirmed it
checks.note: What the party's own law allows may still be forbidden to the lender. The confirmation has to cover both.

checks.question: Does the party screen its customers, suppliers and banks against sanctions lists before it deals with them, under a written policy?
checks.assumption: The party's own screening would find and stop a dealing with a person under sanctions
checks.ask: Do you have a written sanctions policy? How do you check a new customer, supplier or bank against the lists, and how often are existing ones checked again?
checks.note: A policy that is not applied is no protection. Ask to see the record of a recent screening.

indicators.title: Source of the owners' funds
indicators.claim: The money the party puts into the business comes from a source that is known and lawful, and it is the party's own.

matters_more_when.reason: A new project is paid for with fresh equity, so its source has to be shown before it is counted
A large investment programme usually needs new money from the owners

look_again_when.reason: A statement from the time of payment shows where the money in fact came from
A new financing plan can change how much the owners put in, and who

checks.question: Is the party to put money or assets into the business as part of this financing: equity, a shareholder loan, or a promise to pay in later?
checks.why: Opens the topic. The checks on the source are asked only of a party that puts something in. OBS_SOF_005 is asked of every owner.
checks.note: Answer from the sources and uses of the financing plan, not from what the party says alone. Money paid in during the last two years to prepare this financing counts.

checks.question: Has the party stated in writing where that money comes from (which business, sale, inheritance or loan) and from which account it will be paid?
checks.assumption: The party has named the source of the money it puts in
checks.ask: Where does the money you are putting in come from? Please name the source (profits of which business, the sale of which asset, a loan from whom) and the account it will be paid from.
checks.if_unknown: Money whose source is not named cannot be counted as equity.

checks.question: Do the party's accounts, tax returns or other records of its wealth show that it could have earned or saved that amount from the source it names?
checks.assumption: The amount is within what the named source could have produced
checks.note: Set the amount against several years of profit after tax, or against the price in the sale agreement. A source that explains a tenth of the money explains a tenth of it.

checks.question: Do documents from someone other than the party (a bank's statement, a sale agreement, a notary's deed) show the money in the party's own account and coming from the source it names?
checks.assumption: Documents from third parties bear out the source and show the money in the party's own hands
checks.ask: Could we have the documents that show where the money comes from: the bank statements, and the sale agreement or the accounts behind them?

checks.question: Does the money reach the business by a roundabout way: from a third party's account, through several accounts or countries without a business reason, or in cash?
checks.assumption: The money comes straight from the party's own account to the business
checks.note: Look again when the money is paid in: the statement of the receiving account names the sender.

checks.question: Has the party borrowed the money for its stake in the business, or does anyone have a right to get that money back from the party or from the business (a loan to the owner, a put option, a promised return)?
checks.assumption: The party's stake is paid for with its own money, and nobody can claim it back
checks.ask: Did you borrow to fund your stake in the company, or does any investor or lender have a right to be bought out or repaid from it?
checks.note: Equity that is someone else's debt has to be served from dividends, and whoever lent it can end up as the owner. The accounts meant here are the owner's own, not those of the business.

leads_to.reason: An owner with debt of its own needs cash from the business to service it

indicators.title: Management
indicators.claim: The people who run the party have run a business like this before, and it would survive the loss of any one of them.

matters_more_when.reason: A new business has no record of its own: the only record is that of its managers
A turnaround asks more of management than the years that led to it

look_again_when.reason: A new chart can show that a key person has left or that a function has changed hands
A new extract can show a change of directors

checks.question: Has the present management run this business, or one of the same kind and at least the same size, through a bad year: a fall in sales, a collapse in prices or a crisis in its market?
checks.assumption: Management has been tested by a bad year in a business like this one
checks.ask: When was the last bad year for this business, who was in charge then, and what did they do?
checks.note: Where the loan pays for a step up in size or for a new line of business, measure against the business as it will be, not as it is. The accounts of the bad year show how it was handled.

checks.question: Has the chief executive or the head of finance changed in the last two years, and if so, how?
checks.assumption: The people who built the record the lender relies on are still in charge, or handed over in a planned way
checks.flag_when: is unplanned_departure or dismissal_or_dispute or reason_not_known
checks.why: An unplanned change at the top, above all in finance, often comes before bad news in the accounts. A planned handover does not. Two years is the span in which such news usually comes out.
checks.ask: Has your chief executive or head of finance changed in the last two years? Why did the previous one leave, and where is that person now?
checks.note: If both changed, give the worse of the two. A change of auditor in the same period is worth noting beside it.

checks.question: In the last ten years, has the chief executive, the head of finance or the controlling owner led a business that became insolvent or defaulted on its lenders?
checks.assumption: None of those in charge has led a business into insolvency or default in the last ten years
checks.note: Ten years is a guide. A party that says yes is believed: ask what the lenders of that business recovered. If the search finds nothing, record what was searched, where and when.

checks.question: Does the business depend on one or two people for something nobody else at the party could take over within about six months: its main customers, its know-how, its licences or its bank lines?
checks.assumption: The business would carry on if any one person left
checks.ask: If you, or your most important colleague, could not work for six months, who would deal with the main customers, the bank and the technical side?
checks.note: Six months is a guide. Look at whose name is on the customer contracts, the licences and the personal guarantees, and who signs at the bank.

checks.question: Is there a second line of managers who already run finance, operations and sales day to day, without the key person signing off each decision?
checks.assumption: A second line of managers already runs the main functions
checks.note: Titles on a chart are not a second line. Ask who decided the last price change, the last hire and the last large purchase.

checks.question: Is there a written succession plan, approved by the board or the owners, that names who would take over from each key person?
checks.assumption: A named successor stands ready for each key role
checks.ask: Is there a written plan for who would take over from each key person? Has the board approved it, and do the people named know?

checks.question: Is the life and the ability to work of each key person insured, with the party or the lender as beneficiary?
checks.assumption: Insurance would pay the party, or the lender, if a key person died or could no longer work
checks.note: Insurance pays money: it does not replace the person. Set the sum insured against what the party would lose in the year it takes to find someone else.

indicators.title: The accounts
indicators.claim: The party's accounts can be relied on: an independent auditor has signed them without reservation, they cover the companies the lender relies on, and the profit they show was earned in cash.

matters_more_when.reason: The first way out rests on past results, and the accounts are the only record of them
In a group, which companies the accounts cover decides what every figure means
In distress the auditor's view on going concern and the age of the figures matter most

look_again_when.reason: A new year's accounts bring a new audit opinion and can restate the earlier figures
Newer management accounts can part from the last audited figures

checks.question: Has an external auditor audited the party's annual accounts for each of the last three financial years, or for every year since it was formed if that is shorter?
checks.assumption: An external auditor has audited the party's accounts for each of the last three years
checks.ask: Are your annual accounts audited by an outside firm? For which of the last three years can you send us the signed audit report?
checks.if_unknown: Without an audit, every figure in the analysis is the party's own word.
checks.note: The audit report must be signed and dated. A review, a compilation or accounts marked as draft are not an audit. A year that ended less than six months ago, and whose audit is still under way, does not count. Go one year further back. A guarantor who is a natural person has no audited accounts. Answer no for that person, and rely on what The guarantor's capacity finds.

checks.question: Which firm audits the party's accounts, and since which financial year?
checks.why: The weight of an audit depends on who signs it. A firm that is registered, known and has no tie to the owners counts for more than one that nobody can find.
checks.note: Record whether the firm is registered with the audit regulator or the professional body where it works, and any tie between the firm and the party's owners or managers.

checks.question: Is the auditor registered with the body that oversees auditors in its country, does it audit other companies of about the party's size, and is it free of any other tie to the party or its owners (no family tie, no shareholding, no bookkeeping for the party)?
checks.assumption: The auditor is registered, experienced with companies of this size and independent of the party and its owners
checks.why: An audit is worth what the auditor is worth. A one-person firm that is tied to the owner, or that also keeps the party's books, signs what it is given.
checks.ask: Is your audit firm registered with the body that oversees auditors? Which other companies of your size does it audit? Does it, or anyone in it, do other work for you or have a tie to your owners?
checks.note: All three parts must hold for a yes. Say which part fails. Look the firm up in the public register of the audit regulator or the professional body. If a search for ties between the firm and the owners finds nothing, record what was searched, where and when. "About the party's size" is a guide.

checks.question: Does the auditor's report on the latest accounts carry a qualified or adverse opinion, a disclaimer, an emphasis of matter, or a paragraph on doubt that the party can continue as a going concern?
checks.assumption: The auditor's report on the latest accounts is clean, with no modified opinion, no emphasis of matter and no doubt about going concern
checks.note: Read the audit report itself. A summary of the figures, or a set of accounts without the auditor's pages, does not show the opinion. Look at the two years before as well, and say so if a reservation was made then and has since gone.

leads_to.reason: Where the reservation is about going concern, the auditor doubts that the party can pay what falls due

checks.question: Which companies do the accounts used for the analysis cover, set against the party the lender relies on?
checks.assumption: The accounts cover the party the lender relies on, no more and no less
checks.flag_when: is wider_group or part_only or combined_unaudited
checks.why: Accounts of a wider group count the profit and cash of companies that owe the lender nothing. Accounts of a part leave out debts and losses elsewhere in the party. Combined figures that no auditor signed are the party's own word.
checks.ask: Are the accounts you sent us for this company alone, for this company with its subsidiaries, or for a larger group? Which companies are in them, and which are left out?
checks.note: The note on the basis of consolidation lists what is in and what is out. Part only: a division, a branch, or one of several companies that together make up the party. Combined unaudited: figures that management added together for companies that do not report as one. Where consolidated accounts are used, ask for the party's own stand-alone accounts as well.

leads_to.reason: Cash earned in subsidiaries has to come up to the party before it can pay the lender
The lender has to know what the party can claim from the rest of the group, and what the group can take from it

checks.question: How many months have passed since the year-end of the latest audited accounts?
checks.assumption: The latest audited accounts are no more than one audit cycle old
checks.why: An audit is normally signed within about six months of the year-end. More than eighteen months therefore means that a whole year's audit is late or missing, and the lender is reading figures for a business that may have changed. An institution can set its own figure.
checks.note: Count to the day of the answer and give the year-end date. The answer grows older with every month, so look at it again before approval.

checks.question: In the last three years, has the party's auditor resigned, declined to stand again, or been replaced for a reason other than a rotation that the law or the party's own rules require?
checks.assumption: No auditor has left the party early in the last three years
checks.why: An auditor who leaves early has often disagreed with management about the figures. The reason is in the resignation letter and the board minutes, not in the new auditor's report.
checks.ask: Has the same firm audited your accounts in each of the last three years? If not, why did the earlier firm leave?
checks.note: Compare the firm that signed each of the last three audit reports. A party that says yes is believed. A party that says no is believed once the three reports bear it out.

checks.question: In the last three years, has the party restated earlier figures to correct an error, or changed an accounting policy by its own choice, in a way that changed reported profit or equity?
checks.assumption: The figures of the last three years were drawn up on one basis and have not been corrected afterwards
checks.why: A restatement means that earlier accounts were wrong. A change of policy that the party chose (a longer life for its assets, revenue counted earlier, costs moved to the balance sheet) can lift profit without any change in the business.
checks.note: A change that a new accounting standard required of every company is a no. Say what changed, and compare the years on one basis.

leads_to.reason: An error large enough to restate points at the controls over the books

checks.question: In any of the last three years, did items that brought in no cash make up more than about a quarter of profit before tax: revaluations of property or investments, fair-value gains on crops, livestock or other biological assets, unrealised currency gains, or costs and interest capitalised instead of charged to profit?
checks.assumption: The profit the party reports was earned in cash, not written up
checks.why: Debt is serviced from cash. A revaluation gain, or a cost moved to the balance sheet, raises profit and equity and pays nobody.
checks.note: A quarter is a guide. Take the items from the income statement and its notes, and set them against profit before tax of the same year.

leads_to.reason: The cover has to be worked out from cash, with these items taken out

checks.question: Do the party's management accounts for the latest audited year agree with the audited accounts for that year, with every difference of more than a few percent in revenue, profit or debt explained?
checks.assumption: The party's management accounts agree with its audited accounts for the same period
checks.why: After the audited year-end the lender works from management accounts. If they did not match the audit for the year that both cover, the figures since then cannot be taken at face value.
checks.note: A few percent is a guide. A party that keeps no monthly or quarterly accounts cannot show this. Answer no for it and say so.

checks.question: Does the revenue in the accounts agree, within a few percent, with the turnover declared in the party's value added or sales tax returns and with the receipts on its bank statements for the same year?
checks.assumption: The tax returns and the bank statements bear out the revenue in the accounts
checks.why: The tax authority and the bank keep records that the party does not control. Where an audit carries little weight, setting sales against them is how overstated revenue, or a second set of books, is found.
checks.ask: Please send your value added or sales tax returns for the last financial year, as filed, and the statements of all your bank accounts for the same months.
checks.note: A few percent is a guide. Use the returns as filed and the statements of all the party's bank accounts. Allow for sales that carry no value added or sales tax (exports, exempt goods), for the tax itself in the receipts, and for receipts that are not sales (loans, money from the owners). Record each difference and its cause. A party that cannot produce the returns or the statements is a no.

indicators.title: Changes that need a cause
indicators.claim: Every large change in the party's figures over the last three years has a cause that is known and that a document supports.

matters_more_when.reason: The first way out rests on past figures, so a move in them that nobody can explain undermines it
A growing business changes fast, and growth can hide sales that are not collected
In distress the figures move most, and the causes are the ones the lender needs to know

look_again_when.reason: A new year of accounts brings new changes to explain
Interim figures can show a change before the audit does

checks.question: Did the party's revenue rise or fall by about a fifth or more in any of the last three years, without a cause that a document supports?
checks.assumption: Every large move in the party's revenue has a cause that a document supports
checks.why: A jump in revenue can be one large order, a new customer, an acquisition, or sales booked early. A fall can be a lost customer or a lost licence. Each points somewhere else in the analysis.
checks.ask: Revenue moved a good deal between these years. What was behind it, and which document shows that?
checks.note: A fifth is a guide. If there was no such change, answer no and say so. A cause is supported when a contract, a sales record, a bank statement or a note to the audited accounts bears it out. Management's explanation alone is not support.

leads_to.reason: The cause of a move in revenue usually lies with customers, contracts or prices

checks.question: Did the party's gross or operating margin move by about three percentage points or more in any of the last three years, without a cause that a document supports?
checks.assumption: Every large move in the party's margin has a cause that a document supports
checks.why: A margin that moves by several points means that prices, input costs or the mix of products changed, or that costs were moved from one year to another.
checks.note: Three points is a guide. For a trader on thin margins, take a move of about a fifth of the margin itself. If there was no such change, answer no and say so. Management's explanation alone is not support.

leads_to.reason: Whether the margin holds over good years and bad is tested there
The cause of a move in margin often lies with the price of inputs

checks.question: Did the party's receivables or stock, counted in days of sales, grow by about a fifth or more in any of the last three years, without a cause that a document supports?
checks.assumption: Receivables and stock have grown in step with sales, or the cause is known and supported
checks.why: Receivables that outgrow sales can mean customers who are not paying, or sales that were booked and not made. Stock that outgrows sales can mean goods that will not sell at their book value.
checks.note: A fifth is a guide. Compare working capital as days of sales at the start and at the end of the three years. If there was no such change, answer no and say so. Support for a cause is an ageing list, a stock count or a contract with new payment terms. Management's explanation alone is not support.

leads_to.reason: Whether the receivables can be collected and the stock sold is tested there

checks.question: Did the party's debt rise in any of the last three years by more than it spent in that year on fixed assets, acquisitions and added working capital, without a cause that a document supports?
checks.assumption: The money the party borrowed went into assets that are still there
checks.why: Borrowed money that did not go into assets went somewhere else, such as into losses, to the owners or to related parties.
checks.note: Read the cash flow statement for each year. Set new borrowing against capital spending, acquisitions and the change in working capital. If debt did not rise in this way, answer no and say so.

leads_to.reason: What the party owes, and to whom, is set out there
Borrowed money that left the business often went to related parties

checks.question: Did the party's cash from operations fall while its reported profit rose in any of the last three years, without a cause that a document supports?
checks.assumption: The party's cash and its profit have moved together, or the cause of the gap is known and supported
checks.why: Profit that rises while cash falls is profit that has not been paid for. The gap is either tied up in receivables and stock, or it was never there.
checks.note: Compare cash from operations in the cash flow statement with profit before tax, year by year. If the two did not part in this way, answer no and say so.

leads_to.reason: Profit without cash can come from revaluations or from costs moved to the balance sheet
Profit without cash can be tied up in receivables and stock

checks.question: Did the party's equity change in any of the last three years by an amount that the year's profit or loss does not explain (a revaluation, a dividend, capital paid in or taken out, a restatement, a merger), without a cause that a document supports?
checks.assumption: Every move in the party's equity beyond its profit or loss has a cause that a document supports
checks.why: Equity is the cushion under the lender. A revaluation raises it without cash, and capital taken out lowers it without a loss. Either changes what the leverage figures mean.
checks.note: Read the statement of changes in equity for each year. Support for a cause is a shareholder resolution, a valuation report or a note to the audited accounts. If equity moved only by profit or loss, answer no and say so.

leads_to.reason: A revaluation or a restatement bears on how far the accounts can be relied on
Capital taken out goes to the owners, who are related parties

indicators.title: Profitability
indicators.claim: The party earns its margin from its ordinary business, and that margin has held through good years and bad.

matters_more_when.reason: A trader lives on a thin margin, so a small fall takes most of the profit
A manufacturer carries fixed costs, so a fall in volume cuts profit faster than revenue
A projected margin has to be measured against the margin the party has earned before

matters_less_when.reason: A single-purpose company has few costs of its own, and contracts fix most of them

look_again_when.reason: A new year can be the new worst year, or show the margin turning
Interim figures show the margin since the last audit

checks.question: What was the party's gross margin in the latest financial year (gross profit as a share of revenue)?
checks.why: The starting figure. It is read against the party's own worst year (OBS_COST_006) and against others in the same business, not against a fixed level.
checks.ask: What was your gross margin last year, that is gross profit as a percentage of revenue? If you do not have the figure, revenue and cost of sales are enough.
checks.note: Where the accounts show no cost of sales, as for many service businesses, use the operating margin before depreciation and say so.

checks.question: What was the party's lowest gross margin in any of the last five financial years?
checks.why: A margin is read over a whole cycle. The lowest year shows what a bad year looks like for this business.
checks.note: Say which year it was and what caused it. Use the same definition of margin as in OBS_COST_001. For a party with fewer than five years of accounts, say how many years the answer covers.

checks.question: Are the party's costs mostly fixed or mostly variable?
checks.why: A business whose costs are mostly fixed loses profit faster than revenue when volume drops. The answer says how hard a fall in sales would hit.
checks.ask: Which of your costs would stay the same for a year if your sales fell by a quarter (rent, salaried staff, depreciation, interest), and which would fall with them (raw materials, commissions, freight)?
checks.note: Fixed costs are those that stay for a year when volume falls. Mostly means more than about half of all costs: that is a guide.

leads_to.reason: The downside case should show what a fall in volume does to profit when the costs stay

checks.question: Is the party's gross margin in the latest financial year lower than it was two years earlier?
checks.assumption: The party's margin has held over the last two years
checks.ask: What was your gross margin in each of the last three years? If it fell, what was behind the fall?
checks.if_unknown: Without the two earlier years there is no trend, and one year's margin proves little.
checks.note: Use the same definition of gross profit in both years, and give both figures. A difference too small to count in this business (well under one point for most, less for a trader on thin margins) is a no.

leads_to.reason: A falling margin often starts with input costs that could not be passed on
A falling margin can also come from prices that competition has pushed down

checks.question: Did the party make an operating profit (before interest and tax, and without one-off items) in each of the last five financial years?
checks.assumption: The party's ordinary business made a profit in every one of the last five years
checks.why: A margin that holds through good years and bad shows in the worst year. A loss in that year says how little room the lender has.
checks.note: For a party with fewer than five years of accounts, answer for the years there are and say how many.

checks.question: In any of the last three years, did items outside the ordinary business make up more than about a quarter of profit before tax: a gain on the sale of an asset, an insurance payout, a grant, a debt forgiven, or income from investments?
checks.assumption: The party's profit comes from its ordinary business and can be expected again
checks.why: A lender is repaid over years. Profit that came once will not come again to meet the next instalment.
checks.note: A quarter is a guide. Gains that brought in no cash, such as revaluations, are asked about in The accounts (OBS_ACC_008).

indicators.title: Existing debt
indicators.claim: The party has paid its lenders as agreed, and what it already owes is all known to the lender.

matters_more_when.reason: A business in distress has usually already missed a payment or asked for a waiver
Other financing is in place, so the new loan has to fit beside it

look_again_when.reason: A new debt schedule shows the debt at a new date
New accounts can show borrowings, charges or a breach that were not there before

checks.question: Does the party owe money to banks, other lenders, lessors or its shareholders?
checks.why: Opens the topic. A "no" is not the end of it. OBS_DEBT_007 checks it against the accounts and the registry.
checks.ask: Do you owe money to any bank, lender, leasing company or shareholder at the moment? A yes or no is enough to start with.

leads_to.reason: The new covenants have to fit beside the existing ones
A lender with covenants can call its loan before this lender can act

checks.question: What is the total debt outstanding, including leases and shareholder loans?
checks.why: The starting figure for leverage and for debt service.
checks.ask: How much do you owe in total today, to all lenders together? Please include leases and loans from shareholders.
checks.note: Take the figure at its highest point in the year where borrowing is seasonal, and say which date it is for. Say how much of it falls due within twelve months.

checks.question: In the last three years, has the party missed a payment, breached a covenant, asked a lender for a waiver or a standstill, or had a loan rescheduled?
checks.assumption: The party has paid and performed as agreed under its loans
checks.ask: In the last three years, was there any moment when a payment to a lender was late, a covenant was not met, or you asked a lender for more time?
checks.note: A party that says yes is believed. A party that says no is believed once the accounts or a lender bear it out.

checks.question: Do the audited accounts, the security registry or a credit report show borrowings, leases or charges that the party has not mentioned?
checks.assumption: The party has told the lender about all its debt
checks.note: This check does not hang on OBS_DEBT_001, so that the topic cannot close on one answer. If the search finds nothing, record what was searched, where and when.

checks.question: Has the party guaranteed the debt of someone else, or given security for it, for amounts that together come to more than about a tenth of the party's own debt?
checks.assumption: The party answers for little debt other than its own and that of the group that repayment relies on
checks.ask: Have you signed a guarantee for anyone else's borrowing, or pledged any of your assets for it? For example for a sister company, a shareholder or a supplier. For whom, and for how much?
checks.note: A guarantee or security for the debt of a member of the group that repayment relies on does not count: that debt is already counted as the group's own. A tenth is a guide to what matters. What counts is whether the party could pay if the guarantee were called and still service its own debt. Below the guide the answer is no: record for whom, how much and what share of the party's own debt in the reason. Count the full amounts guaranteed, not what is drawn today.

checks.question: Is the party's debt that falls due within twelve months larger than its stock and trade receivables together, so that part of it finances fixed assets, losses or loans to others?
checks.assumption: Debt that falls due within a year finances only stock and receivables that turn into cash within the year
checks.why: Short-term lines that finance stock and receivables are repaid when the goods are sold and the customers pay. Short-term debt that paid for a building or covered a loss has nothing to repay it when it falls due.
checks.ask: How much of your debt falls due within the next twelve months, and what does it finance?
checks.note: Count overdrafts, lines that come up for renewal within the year and the part of long-term loans that falls due within it. Take debt, stock and receivables at the same date, and at the seasonal peak of borrowing where there is one. Record the three figures.

checks.question: Have the lenders concerned confirmed in writing that the missed payment or breach is cured or waived?
checks.assumption: The lenders concerned have confirmed that the default is cured or waived
checks.note: The letter must come from the lender concerned. The party's own account of it is not a confirmation.

indicators.title: Cash flow against debt service
indicators.claim: The party's own cash flow covers the service of all its debt, this loan included, with room to spare in a bad year.

matters_more_when.reason: Without security the party's cash flow is the only way out
The cover then rests on a forecast, not on cash that has already been earned
Senior lenders are paid first, so the cover has to hold after their debt service

look_again_when.reason: A new year of cash flow changes the cover, and can be the new worst year
New or repaid debt changes what falls due
A change in amount, tenor, grace period or repayment profile changes the debt service

checks.question: How much cash did the party generate in the last financial year that was free to service debt: cash from operations after tax, after the change in working capital and after the capital spending needed to keep the business as it is, before interest and repayments?
checks.why: The top line of the cover. It starts from cash, not from profit, and takes off what must be spent before any lender is paid.
checks.note: Take the figure from the cash flow statement. Leave out revaluations and other gains without cash, and money raised from new debt or new shares. Say which year and which currency. For a business with no full year behind it, use the first full year of the lender's base case and say so.

checks.question: How much interest and principal must the party pay on all its debt, this loan included, in the first full year in which this loan is being repaid?
checks.why: The bottom line of the cover. The first year after any grace period is used, because a year in which only interest is paid flatters the cover.
checks.ask: Please send a schedule of all your loans and leases that shows, year by year, the interest and the principal that fall due on each.
checks.note: Include lease payments, and shareholder loans that must be paid. Take the interest on seasonal lines at the amounts drawn through the year, not at the year-end balance. Leave out the principal of revolving lines that are committed beyond the year, and say so.

checks.question: How many times did the party's cash flow available for debt service in the last financial year cover the debt service of the first full year of repayment, this loan included?
checks.assumption: Last year's cash flow covers the service of all the party's debt, this loan included, with room to spare
checks.why: Below 1.0 the party could not have paid from its own cash flow. At 1.2 the cash flow can fall by a sixth before a payment is missed, and lenders to operating businesses commonly look for that much or more. It is a convention. A business with contracted revenue can carry less, and one that sells at market prices needs more. An institution can set its own figure.
checks.if_unknown: Until the cover is worked out, nobody has shown that the loan can be repaid from cash flow.
checks.note: Divide the answer to OBS_DS_001 by the answer to OBS_DS_002. A cover worked out from EBITDA (profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), before tax, working capital and capital spending, is not this figure. The test does not wait for the terms of the loan. If the cover is already below the reference point on the debt the party owes today, record that figure now and say that it is before the new loan. Record it again when the terms are known.

checks.question: In the lender's base case, what is the lowest yearly cover of debt service by cash flow available for debt service over the life of the loan?
checks.assumption: In every year of the base case the cash flow covers debt service with room to spare
checks.why: The same convention as OBS_DS_003. Lenders to projects with contracted revenue commonly size the debt at about this level or higher, and ask for more where revenue follows the market. An institution can set its own figure.
checks.if_unknown: Until the lowest cover is known, nobody has shown that the loan can be repaid from cash flow in every year.
checks.note: Say which year the lowest cover falls in. Work out the cash flow as in OBS_DS_001 and the debt service as in OBS_DS_002, year by year. The base case is the lender's own, or one an independent adviser has checked. The party's model as received is the party's own word. If no such case has been run, the check stays open.

checks.question: Would the party's cash flow available for debt service in the worst of the last five financial years have covered that same debt service in full?
checks.assumption: The cash flow of a bad year still covers the service of all the party's debt
checks.why: The claim is about a bad year, not an average one. The party's own worst recent year is a bad year that has already happened.
checks.note: For a party with fewer than five years of accounts, answer for the years there are and say how many. Where the business has changed so much that those years say little, say so. The downside case in Projections and downside then carries the test. The test does not wait for the terms of the loan. If the answer already goes against the assumption on the debt the party owes today, record it now and say that it is before the new loan. Answer again when the terms are known.

leads_to.reason: The downside case shows whether such a year would lead to a missed payment under this loan

checks.question: What is the party's total debt after this loan, as a multiple of its EBITDA (profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) of the last financial year?
checks.assumption: After this loan the party owes no more than about four years of its EBITDA
checks.why: Bank supervisors in the euro area and in the United States use total debt above about four times EBITDA to mark out leveraged lending. Four is a guide for an operating company: read it against what businesses of this kind carry. An institution can set its own figure.
checks.note: Count all borrowing, leases and shareholder loans that must be repaid, without taking cash off. Take the debt at its highest point in the year, not at the year-end. Take EBITDA without one-off items. Record in the reason the multiple before the loan, and the multiple on net debt (after the cash the party is free to use). The test does not wait for the terms of the loan. If the multiple is already above the reference point on the debt the party owes today, record that figure now and say that it is before the new loan. Record it again when the terms are known.

checks.question: Over the last three financial years taken together, was the party's cash from operations (before interest and tax) less than about two thirds of its EBITDA (profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation)?
checks.assumption: The party's profit turns into cash
checks.why: EBITDA counts sales that are not yet collected and stock that is not yet sold. Where cash from operations stays well below it for years, profit is booked that does not arrive, or growth is using it up.
checks.note: Two thirds is a guide. Three years are taken together so that one year's swing in working capital does not decide the answer.

leads_to.reason: The gap between profit and cash usually sits in receivables and stock

checks.question: Do the loan terms require a debt service reserve account that is funded in cash before the first repayment, holds at least the next payment of interest and principal, and is pledged to the lender?
checks.assumption: A funded reserve pays the lender while the party's cash flow recovers
checks.note: A reserve buys time for one or two payments. It does not mend a cash flow that stays short.

checks.question: Has an owner or sponsor undertaken in writing to pay in cash when the party's cash flow falls short of its debt service?
checks.assumption: An owner or sponsor has bound itself to cover a shortfall in debt service
checks.ask: If cash flow fell short of a loan payment, would a shareholder be willing to sign an undertaking to put in the missing cash? Who would sign it?
checks.note: A statement that the owner stands behind the party, with no promise to pay, is a no.

leads_to.reason: The undertaking counts only as far as the lender can enforce it and the giver can pay

indicators.title: Bank: capital
indicators.claim: The institution's capital can absorb the losses its loan book is likely to bring and still stay above the regulatory minimum.

matters_more_when.reason: A subordinated loan to a bank takes losses itself once the capital is gone
Growth in lending uses up capital faster than profit rebuilds it

look_again_when.reason: A new prudential return shows the ratio at a new date, and the regulator can set a new minimum
New accounts show equity, provisions and the dividends paid

checks.question: What is the institution's total capital adequacy ratio (regulatory capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets) at its latest reporting date?
checks.why: The starting figure. It is read against the minimum the regulator sets (OBS_FIC_002) and against what the loan book may still cost (OBS_FIC_006).
checks.ask: What was your capital adequacy ratio at your latest reporting date? Your latest prudential return would answer this.
checks.note: Say which date the figure is for, and whether it is for the institution alone or for its group. Record the tier 1 ratio beside it. Tier 1 is the capital that takes losses while the institution is still running. Where the regulator does not use risk weights, give equity as a percentage of total assets and say so.

checks.question: By how many percentage points does the total capital adequacy ratio exceed the minimum the regulator requires of this institution, with all buffers and any add-on set for it alone?
checks.assumption: The capital ratio stands further above the regulatory minimum than one bad year of loan losses would take away
checks.why: At the minimum the supervisor can stop new lending and dividends, and a breach is an event of default under most loans to banks. Two percentage points of risk-weighted assets is about what a bank loses when three or four percent of its loans go bad and half of that is never recovered. With less headroom, one bad year takes the institution to the minimum. Two points is a guide, not a rule. An institution can set its own figure.
checks.ask: What minimum capital ratio does your regulator require of you, with all buffers? What was your ratio at each quarter-end of the last year?
checks.note: Take the lowest quarter-end of the last twelve months, not the year-end alone. A negative answer means the institution is below the minimum.

checks.question: If the non-performing loans that are not covered by provisions were written off against capital today, would the capital adequacy ratio stay above the regulatory minimum?
checks.assumption: Capital stays above the minimum after the bad loans that are not provided for are taken off
checks.note: Take the non-performing loans less the provisions held against them, and take that amount off both capital and risk-weighted assets. Collateral is left out on purpose, because it is realised late and for less than its book value. Where restructured loans are counted as performing (OBS_FIP_004), work the answer out a second time with them added, and record both.

leads_to.reason: The size of the hole depends on how the loans are classified and provided for

checks.question: Set against its profit and its capital headroom, how much has the institution paid out to its shareholders over the last three financial years?
checks.assumption: The institution keeps most of its profit as capital
checks.why: Retained profit is the main source of new capital for most banks. An institution that pays out most of its profit, or pays out while its headroom is thin, cannot carry its own growth or absorb a bad year. It also shows that its owners take cash out before they build the cushion.
checks.ask: What dividends have you paid in each of the last three years? Do you have a rule that ties dividends to your capital ratio?
checks.note: The options: no_dividends is nothing paid out in the three years. conservative is less than about a third of profit. moderate is between a third and two thirds. aggressive is more than about two thirds of profit, or any payout in a year in which the institution made a loss or its capital ratio was within two percentage points of the minimum. The fractions are a guide. Count share buy-backs as payouts.

checks.question: Does the institution's business plan keep its capital adequacy ratio above the regulatory minimum in every year of the plan, counting only retained profit and new capital that is already committed in writing?
checks.assumption: The capital the institution has, or is sure to get, can carry the growth in lending it plans
checks.ask: How fast do you plan to grow your loan book over the next three years? Please send the capital plan that shows your capital ratio in each of those years.
checks.if_unknown: Without a capital plan nobody has shown that growth will not take the institution to the minimum.
checks.note: Set the profit the plan expects against the profit of the last three years (see Bank, earnings). A plan that needs new capital from shareholders who have not committed to it is a no. A capital plan filed with the supervisor counts as best evidence. The institution's own plan does not.

checks.question: Does part of the institution's regulatory capital consist of subordinated debt (tier 2 capital)?
checks.why: To have none is no fault. Where there is some, it takes losses only once the institution has failed. Under the Basel rules it also counts for less in each of its last five years, so its maturity dates show when the capital ratio will fall without any loss.
checks.ask: Does any subordinated debt count towards your regulatory capital? If so, from whom, how much, and when does each loan fall due?
checks.note: Record the amounts, the lenders and the maturity dates. Where the loan under review is itself meant to count as tier 2 capital, say so.

checks.question: Have the shareholders bound themselves in writing to pay in new capital of a stated amount by a stated date (a signed subscription, a rights issue that is approved and underwritten, or a support undertaking)?
checks.assumption: The shareholders are bound to pay in the capital that is missing
checks.note: A letter of comfort, or a statement that the shareholders stand behind the institution, is a no. Whether the shareholders can pay is asked in Owner and group.

leads_to.reason: A promise of capital is worth what the shareholder can pay

indicators.title: Bank: earnings
indicators.claim: The institution's lasting earnings cover its loan losses, in a bad year too, and leave a profit that adds to its capital.

matters_more_when.reason: A growing institution needs its profit as capital for the new lending
A subordinated lender is paid only while the institution earns enough to keep its capital whole

look_again_when.reason: A new year of earnings and loan-loss charges can be the new worst year
Half-year figures show a turn in the margin or in loan losses before the annual accounts do

checks.question: What was the institution's return on average assets (profit after tax as a percentage of average total assets) in the last financial year?
checks.why: The headline measure of a bank's earnings. It is read against the last three years, against the banks in its market, and against the growth of the balance sheet. Profit that does not keep pace with that growth does not build capital.
checks.note: Say which year the figure is for. Where inflation is high, record it beside the figure, because a return below inflation shrinks the capital in real terms.

checks.question: Would the institution's profit before loan-loss charges and tax of the last financial year have covered a loan-loss charge as heavy, as a share of the loan book, as in the worst of its last five financial years?
checks.assumption: The institution's earnings absorb a bad year of loan losses without a loss
checks.why: Profit before loan-loss charges is the first cushion. What it cannot absorb comes out of capital. The institution's own worst recent year is a bad year that has already happened.
checks.note: Take the loan-loss charge of each year as a percentage of average gross loans, and apply the highest to today's loan book. With fewer than five years of accounts, use the years there are and say how many. Where the provisions have been short (OBS_FIP_002), the past charges understate the cost. Say so.

leads_to.reason: A loss comes straight out of capital

checks.question: Over the last three financial years, has the institution's net interest margin (net interest income as a percentage of average earning assets) widened, held or narrowed?
checks.why: The margin is where a bank's profit starts. A margin that narrows means dearer funding, cheaper lending or more loans that pay no interest, and each of them points to another indicator. A margin that widens fast can mean riskier lending.
checks.note: Stable means a change of less than about a quarter of a percentage point over the three years. Record the margin of each year.

leads_to.reason: Dearer funding is a common cause of a narrowing margin, and it shows which funding the institution has to pay up for

checks.question: What was the institution's cost-to-income ratio (operating costs before loan-loss charges, as a percentage of operating income) in the last financial year?
checks.why: The ratio says how much of each unit of income is left to pay for loan losses and to build capital. It is read against banks of the same kind in the same market. A branch network that serves small borrowers costs more than a bank that lends to large companies.

checks.question: Did more than about a third of the institution's profit before tax in the last financial year come from gains that need not come again: trading and revaluation gains, currency gains, the sale of assets, or the release of provisions?
checks.assumption: The profit comes from lending and fees, which come again each year
checks.note: A third is a guide. Where the institution would have made a loss without such gains, the answer is yes. Look at each of the last three years. A one-off that comes back every year under another name is still not income from lending.

checks.question: In the last financial year, was more than about a tenth of the institution's interest income booked but not received in cash (interest accrued on loans in arrears or under a grace period, or added to the loan balance)?
checks.assumption: The interest the institution reports as income is paid to it in cash
checks.why: Interest that is booked and not paid is profit on paper. It raises capital in the accounts without adding any, and it grows fastest when borrowers are in trouble.
checks.note: A tenth is a guide. Set the interest income in the profit and loss account against the interest received in the cash flow statement, and the growth of accrued interest receivable against the growth of the loan book. Loans with long grace periods (to farmers, to projects) accrue interest by design. Say so, and record what happened when earlier grace periods ended.

indicators.title: Bank: loan quality
indicators.claim: The losses in the institution's loan book are no larger than its accounts show, and no single sector or group of borrowers could bring a loss that its capital cannot take.

matters_more_when.reason: A fast-growing loan book is young, and its bad loans have not yet shown
An institution under strain has every reason to put off recognising its bad loans

look_again_when.reason: New accounts show the classification of loans, the provisions and the write-offs at a new date
An inspection can reclassify loans and order more provisions
A new portfolio report shows arrears and restructured loans at a new date

checks.question: What share of the institution's gross loans is non-performing at its latest reporting date?
checks.why: The headline figure of loan quality. It is read against the institution's own past, against the banks in its market, and against what the other checks say about how loans are classified.
checks.ask: What share of your loan book is non-performing today, and how do you define non-performing? Your latest prudential return would answer this.
checks.note: Say which date the figure is for. Record beside it the loans written off in each of the last three years as a share of the book, because a low ratio after heavy write-offs is not a clean book. Portfolio at risk over thirty days, which microfinance institutions report, is a different and stricter measure. Say which one is given.

checks.question: Does the institution count as non-performing every loan on which a payment is more than ninety days overdue?
checks.assumption: Loans that have stopped paying are counted as bad loans
checks.why: Ninety days is the international convention (the Basel Committee's definition of default). An institution that waits longer, or that counts only the overdue instalment and not the whole loan, reports fewer bad loans than it has.
checks.ask: After how many days in arrears do you classify a loan as non-performing? Do you then classify the whole loan, or only the instalments that are overdue?
checks.note: Read the accounting policy note and the credit policy, then check them against the arrears report. The balance of loans more than ninety days overdue should not be larger than the reported non-performing loans. The whole outstanding balance of a loan counts, not only the instalments in arrears.

checks.question: What share of the gross loan book consists of loans that were rescheduled, refinanced or otherwise restructured because the borrower could not pay as agreed, and that are counted as performing?
checks.assumption: Few loans are kept out of the bad-loan figure by restructuring them
checks.why: Loans restructured because the borrower could not pay are the first place where bad loans hide. They are counted as performing and carry little provision. The European Banking Authority's guidelines ask banks in the European Union whose non-performing loans reach five percent of their loans to adopt a plan to reduce them. Other supervisors use other levels. Where the restructured loans alone reach that size, the reported ratio says little. Five percent is a guide. An institution can set its own figure.
checks.ask: What share of your loan book has been rescheduled or refinanced because the borrower could not pay as first agreed? How do you classify such loans afterwards?
checks.if_unknown: An institution that cannot say how much of its book is restructured does not know its own bad loans.
checks.note: Include loans repaid with a new loan from the institution, loans on which unpaid interest was added to the balance, and loans given a grace period after they fell into arrears. Record the figure for each of the last three years.

checks.question: Do the institution's loan-loss provisions alone cover at least about half of its non-performing loans, and do provisions together with collateral at its forced-sale value cover them in full?
checks.assumption: The loss in the non-performing loans is provided for
checks.ask: What provisions do you hold against your non-performing loans, and what collateral? When was the collateral last valued, and by whom?
checks.note: Count only collateral that the institution holds under a registered charge and that an independent valuer has valued within the last two years. Record the coverage ratio (provisions as a percentage of non-performing loans) as well. Where the supervisor or the auditor has asked for more provisions, the answer is no. Half is a guide. An institution can set its own figure.

leads_to.reason: What is not provided for comes out of capital

checks.question: Does the institution have a written policy that fixes when a non-performing loan must be written off, and do its write-offs of the last two years follow it?
checks.assumption: Bad loans are written off under a fixed rule, neither kept on the books nor removed to flatter the figures
checks.ask: When do you write a loan off, and who decides? Please send the policy and the list of write-offs of the last two years.
checks.note: Set the write-offs of the last two years against the policy. Loans written off earlier than the policy says lower the bad-loan ratio. Loans kept beyond it overstate the assets. Ask whether written-off loans were sold or moved to a related party, and at what price.

checks.question: Over the last three years, has the institution's loan book grown at more than about twice the rate of bank lending in its market?
checks.assumption: The loan book has grown at a pace at which its quality can already be seen
checks.why: Loans go bad a year or two after they are made. A book that grows fast is young, so its bad-loan ratio stays low for a while whatever the lending is like. Fast growth is also often won by taking the borrowers that other banks turned down.
checks.note: Twice is a guide. Take the growth of the market from the central bank's published figures, and say which figures were used. Growth by buying another institution or a portfolio is growth all the same.

checks.question: Does any one economic sector, or any one region, account for more than about a quarter of the loan book?
checks.assumption: No single sector or region could, by its own downturn, turn a large part of the loan book bad
checks.ask: How is your loan book spread over sectors and regions? Which is the largest of each, and what share of the book does it hold?
checks.note: A quarter is a guide. An institution built to serve one sector or one region (an agricultural bank, a regional microfinance institution) will answer yes. Then record how that sector or region fared in its last bad year. Sort loans by what the borrower's cash flow depends on, not by the label in the institution's system. Single borrowers are asked in OBS_FIP_007.

checks.question: Do the institution's ten largest exposures, with connected borrowers counted as one, add up to more than its regulatory capital?
checks.assumption: The failure of a handful of large borrowers would not take away the institution's capital
checks.ask: Please send the list of your twenty largest exposures, with borrowers that belong together shown as one group, and each as a percentage of your capital.
checks.note: Ten exposures and the whole of capital are a guide. Count loans, guarantees and undrawn commitments. Record the largest single exposure as a share of capital, and whether it is within the limit the regulator sets for one borrower. Ask how the institution decides which borrowers are connected.

checks.question: Are more than about half of the institution's loans in foreign currency owed by borrowers who do not earn that currency?
checks.assumption: The institution lends foreign currency mainly to borrowers who earn it
checks.why: A borrower who earns local currency and owes foreign currency owes more after a devaluation and earns the same. The institution's own currency position can be matched while its borrowers carry the mismatch, and their losses come back to it as bad loans.
checks.ask: What share of your loan book is in foreign currency? How much of that is lent to borrowers who earn that currency, such as exporters, and how do you establish it?
checks.if_unknown: An institution that does not know which of its borrowers earn the currency they borrow in cannot say what a devaluation would do to its loan book.
checks.note: Half is a guide. Record the share of the whole loan book that is in foreign currency. A borrower earns the currency where its sales are paid in it. Loans in local currency whose amount follows the exchange rate count as foreign currency. Where the institution lends no foreign currency, answer no and say so.

indicators.title: Projections and downside
indicators.claim: The projections rest on assumptions that can be checked against the party's own record, and debt service is still paid when revenue, margin and timing are as bad as the party has seen.

matters_more_when.reason: The first way out is a forecast, so the forecast is what the lender is lending against
A new business has no record to hold the forecast against
Repayment counts on capacity that is not yet built

look_again_when.reason: A new version of the model can change the assumptions and the downside
A new year of actual figures shows whether the forecast was met
Interim figures show whether the current year is on budget

checks.question: Has the party prepared financial projections (a financial model, a business plan with figures, or a budget for several years)?
checks.why: Opens the topic. A no does not close it. The party's record against its own budget (OBS_PROJ_008) and the downside case (OBS_PROJ_006) are asked either way.
checks.ask: Have you prepared financial projections, such as a financial model, a business plan with projected figures or a budget for the coming years? A yes or no is enough to start with.

checks.question: What period do the projections cover?
checks.why: A forecast that stops before the loan is repaid says nothing about the last payments.
checks.note: Set the period against the life of this loan, and say whether the projections reach the final repayment.

checks.question: Are the assumptions behind the projections written down, so that each can be checked against a source: volumes, prices, costs, capital spending, working capital, interest and exchange rates?
checks.assumption: The projections rest on assumptions that are written down and can be checked
checks.ask: Can you send us the assumptions behind your projections, with the source of each? In a model this is usually the assumptions sheet.
checks.note: Figures typed into the model with no source are not written down in this sense.

checks.question: Has someone independent of the party, and of whoever built the projections, reviewed them: the arithmetic of the model and the sources of its inputs?
checks.assumption: Someone independent of the party has tested the projections
checks.ask: Has anyone outside your company reviewed the projections, for example a model auditor or a financial adviser? Can we see the report?
checks.note: A model audit or an independent adviser's review counts. So does the lender's own rebuild of the figures, if it is written down. The auditor's signature on past accounts does not.

checks.question: How do the revenue growth and the margin in the projections compare with what the party achieved in the last five years?
checks.assumption: The projections ask for nothing the party has not achieved before
checks.why: A forecast above the party's own best years asks the lender to believe in a business that has not existed yet. Repayment then depends on the improvement, not on the record.
checks.note: Aggressive: growth or margin in any projected year is above the best of the last five years. In line: both stay within the range of those years. Conservative: both stay at or below their average. For a business with no history, compare with businesses of the same kind and say which.

checks.question: Did the party's revenue or operating profit in the last financial year fall short of its own budget or forecast for that year by more than about a tenth?
checks.assumption: The party has met its own forecasts
checks.why: The best test of a forecast is the forecaster's record. A party that missed its own budget by a wide margin last year is asking the lender to trust the next one.
checks.ask: What budget did your board approve for last year, and how did revenue and operating profit turn out against it? Please send the budget as it was approved.
checks.note: A tenth is a guide. Use the budget that was approved before the year began, not a later revision. A party that set no budget has no record to show. Leave the check open for it and say so.

checks.question: Is all debt service still paid when due in a downside case that sets revenue, margin and timing no better than the worst the party has seen in the last five years?
checks.assumption: Debt service is still paid in a downside case
checks.why: The base case is what the party hopes for. The lender is repaid in the case that happens.
checks.if_unknown: Nobody knows how much can go wrong before a payment is missed.
checks.note: A case that trims the base case by a few percent is not a downside. For a business without five years behind it, use the worst that businesses of the same kind have seen and say which. Run the case with this facility drawn in full and with the existing debt. If no such case has been run, the check stays open.

leads_to.reason: The amount and the profile of the loan can still be changed

checks.question: By what share can revenue fall below the base case, with costs behaving as they did in the party's past, before a payment of debt service is missed?
checks.why: The room for error, in one figure. It is read against the largest fall in revenue the party has had in a year.
checks.note: Give the lowest figure over the life of the loan, and the year it falls in.

indicators.title: Tax
indicators.claim: The party owes no tax it has not provided for, and its cash flow does not depend on a tax position that can be taken away before the loan is repaid.

matters_more_when.reason: A business short of cash often stops paying the tax authority before it stops paying anyone else
In a group, prices and loans between companies in different countries draw the tax authorities' attention
Projected cash flow may count on a tax holiday or a reduced rate that does not last

look_again_when.reason: A clearance certificate is good for a short time only
A notice or an assessment from the tax authority changes what is owed
New accounts show new tax provisions and contingent liabilities

checks.question: Has the party filed every tax return that fell due in the last three years: income tax, value added or sales tax, and payroll taxes?
checks.assumption: The party has filed its tax returns when due
checks.ask: Are all your tax returns for the last three years filed (income tax, value added or sales tax, payroll taxes)? A tax clearance certificate, or the filed returns with proof of filing, would show it.
checks.if_unknown: Years for which no return is filed stay open to assessment, and nobody knows for how much.
checks.note: A party that is not registered with the tax authority in its own name is a no.

checks.question: Does the party owe tax that is past its due date, or is it paying off tax arrears under a plan agreed with the tax authority?
checks.assumption: The party has paid its taxes when due
checks.why: Unpaid tax is borrowing from the state without its consent. A business that falls behind on tax is usually short of cash, and the tax authority can often collect faster than a lender.
checks.ask: Is any tax overdue at the moment, or are you paying off older tax in instalments agreed with the tax authority?
checks.note: Look for tax payable in the balance sheet that grows from year to year, and for penalties and interest on tax in the income statement. Whether the tax authority ranks ahead of the lender is a question for counsel in the country concerned.

leads_to.reason: Tax arrears are a sign that cash is short

checks.question: In the last three years, has the tax authority raised an additional assessment against the party, or is a tax dispute open now, for an amount (with penalties and interest) above about a tenth of the party's yearly profit before tax?
checks.assumption: The tax authority claims no amount from the party, beyond what the party declared, that would take more than about a tenth of a year's profit
checks.ask: Has the tax authority audited you in the last three years, asked for more tax than you declared, or is any audit or dispute still open? What amounts are involved?
checks.if_unknown: An open tax claim of unknown size sits outside every figure in the analysis.
checks.note: A routine audit with no assessment is a no. Record it in the reason. A tenth is a guide. Say which years an audit covered and whether it is closed. Record the amount of every assessment or dispute, also one below the guide. The notes on contingent liabilities in the audited accounts list open tax claims. If a search of court or tax registers finds nothing, record what was searched, where and when.

leads_to.reason: An open tax dispute is a claim against the party like any other

checks.question: Does the party save more than about a tenth of a year's profit through a tax holiday, an exemption or a reduced rate that ends before this loan is repaid, or that depends on conditions the party is not meeting now (a level of investment, jobs or exports)?
checks.assumption: The tax savings that matter to the party's cash flow last as long as the loan
checks.why: When a tax holiday ends, tax takes a share of the cash flow that the loan was sized on. A regime that is granted on conditions is lost when the conditions are not kept.
checks.note: A tenth of a year's profit before tax is a guide to what matters. A regime that saves less is a no: record what it is, what it saves in a year and when it ends. Compare the tax the party pays with the standard rate on its profit. A wide gap means that a special regime is at work, whether or not the party has mentioned one. Check that the projections charge the full rate from the day the regime ends. Where the party does not meet the conditions now, the answer is yes whatever the tenor of the loan turns out to be: record it now.

leads_to.reason: The projections have to charge tax in full from the day the regime ends

checks.question: Does tax arise across a border in the party's dealings: tax withheld on interest, dividends or fees, prices set with related parties abroad, or a taxable presence in another country?
checks.why: Tax across a border takes cash on its way to the lender or on its way up from a subsidiary. Prices between related parties in different countries are what tax authorities challenge most often.
checks.ask: Do you pay or receive interest, dividends, fees or the price of goods across a border, in particular to or from companies in your own group? Is tax withheld on any of these payments?
checks.note: Where interest on this loan will be paid across a border, find out whether tax is withheld on it, at what rate, and whether the loan terms make the party pay it on top.

leads_to.reason: Who bears tax withheld on interest paid to the lender is a term of the loan
Prices and loans between the party and related parties abroad are tested there

checks.question: Is the full amount that the tax authority claims, with penalties and interest, either paid or provided for in the latest audited accounts?
checks.assumption: What the tax authority claims is already paid or counted in the accounts
checks.note: A provision is the party's own estimate. Set it against the amount in the tax authority's notice.

indicators.title: Bank: funding and liquidity
indicators.claim: The institution can meet withdrawals and repay the funding that falls due, in each currency it owes, without selling assets at a loss.

matters_more_when.reason: Depositors and other banks leave first when there is doubt, and a bank fails on the day it cannot pay them
An unsecured lender is repaid from the same liquid assets that depositors draw on

look_again_when.reason: A new prudential return shows the liquidity ratios and the open currency position at a new date
The maturity table and the funding notes show who funds the institution and until when
Monthly figures show deposits leaving before the annual accounts do

checks.question: What are the institution's liquid assets (cash, balances at the central bank above the required reserve, balances at other banks that are repayable within a month, and government securities that are not pledged) as a percentage of its customer deposits and other funding repayable within twelve months?
checks.why: The first cushion against withdrawals. It is read against the regulatory minimum (OBS_FIL_006), against the institution's own lowest point of the year, and against how concentrated and how short its funding is.
checks.ask: What liquid assets do you hold today, and what are they as a share of your deposits and other short-term funding? Your latest prudential return would answer this.
checks.note: Regulators define the liquid asset ratio in different ways. Give the figure as the question defines it, and record beside it the regulator's own ratio and, where it is reported, the liquidity coverage ratio. Say which date the figures are for.

checks.question: Has the institution met every liquidity requirement its regulator sets (such as a liquid asset ratio, a liquidity coverage ratio and the reserve requirement) at every reporting date of the last twelve months?
checks.assumption: The institution has kept its liquidity above the regulatory minimum throughout the year
checks.ask: Which liquidity ratios does your regulator require, and at what level? Please send your returns for each month of the last year.
checks.note: Ask for the returns of every month or quarter, not for the year-end alone, because a ratio is easily dressed for one day. Where the regulator sets no liquidity requirement, say so, and answer against the limit the institution's own board has set.

checks.question: Do the twenty largest depositors hold more than about a quarter of the institution's deposits?
checks.assumption: No small group of depositors could drain the institution by leaving
checks.ask: What share of your deposits do your twenty largest depositors hold? How much of it could be withdrawn within a month?
checks.note: Twenty depositors and a quarter are a guide. Count connected depositors as one, and count the deposits of the state and of state bodies together, because they move on one decision. An institution that takes no deposits is a no. Its funding is tested in OBS_FIL_007.

checks.question: Are the institution's loans larger than its customer deposits, its funding with more than a year left to run and its equity taken together?
checks.assumption: The loans are funded by money that stays, namely deposits, long-term funding and equity
checks.why: Loans cannot be called in when funding leaves. Where loans exceed the funding that stays, the difference is financed by money that must be renewed within a year, and the institution depends on its lenders being willing every time.
checks.note: Take the figures from the maturity table in the notes to the accounts, by the time left to run and not by the original term. Where the institution reports a net stable funding ratio, a ratio below 100 percent is a yes. Where OBS_FIL_002 found the deposits concentrated, they are less sure to stay than this test takes them to be.

checks.question: Does the wholesale funding that falls due within twelve months (loans from banks, funds and development lenders, bonds and money-market borrowing, at home and abroad) exceed the institution's unpledged liquid assets?
checks.assumption: The institution could repay the wholesale funding that falls due within a year even if none of it were renewed
checks.why: Wholesale lenders are few, well informed and quick. They do not renew when there is doubt, and funding from abroad can stop for reasons that have nothing to do with the institution, such as a downgrade of the country or a shortage of foreign currency.
checks.ask: Please send a list of your borrowings from banks, funds and other lenders, with the amount, the currency and the date on which each falls due.
checks.note: Include the part of long-term loans that falls due within the year, and loans that a lender can call early because a covenant is breached. Record separately what is owed in foreign currency and the liquid assets held in that currency. Local-currency cash does not repay a foreign-currency loan when foreign currency is scarce.

checks.question: What share of the institution's total funding (all its liabilities) is owed to other banks: interbank deposits, money-market borrowing and repurchase agreements?
checks.why: Other banks are the first to withdraw. A high or a rising share means that the institution cannot fund itself from its customers.
checks.ask: How much do you owe to other banks today, and for how long is it lent to you? Has that amount grown or shrunk over the last three years?
checks.note: Record how long the bulk of it has left to run (overnight, under three months, longer) and the figure for each of the last three years. Record also what the institution has placed with other banks, and with which. That side is a credit exposure, and the largest of them count among the large exposures in OBS_FIP_007.
